cluster.headline: מאות שנים אחרי: ישראלי גילה ממה מתה מלכת שבדיה חוקרים ובהם פרופ' עבאסי מהטכניון מציעים פתרון לתעלומת מותה של כריסטינה, שוויתרה על הכתר: סוכרת שלא אובחנה צור גואטה

primary_source.title: Barth RF, Buja LM, Abassi Z. 'Drottning Kristina: Omvärdering av sjukdomshistoria och dödsorsak' (Queen Christina: a reassessment of her medical history and cause of death), Läkartidningen (Swedish Medical Journal), published 11 March 2026 in the journal's Kultur / Medicinhistoria (culture / medical-history) section — a retrospective-diagnosis essay, not original peer-reviewed laboratory research. Authors in published order: (1) Rolf F Barth, Department of Pathology, The Ohio State University; (2) L Maximilian Buja, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston; (3) Zaid Abassi, Department of Physiology and Biophysics, Ruth and Bruce Rappaport Faculty of Medicine, Technion — Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa, and Rambam Health Care Campus. Occasioned by the 400th anniversary of Christina's birth (b. 1626). METHODOLOGY: re-examination of surviving historical and biographical records, symptoms documented by contemporaries during her lifetime (extreme thirst, excessive urination, weight loss, recurrent chronic leg wounds), and the findings of the postmortem examination performed at the Riario Palace in Rome by her court physician/surgeon Alessio Spalla three days after her death on 19 April 1689. No new physical material was examined; the 1965 exhumation and skeletal examination of her remains was inconclusive as to which illnesses she had suffered. CONCLUSION (hedged): Christina 'most likely' suffered from undiagnosed diabetes, which 'may have contributed' to a chronic wound and bacterial infection of her right leg (diagnosed at the time as erysipelas), the infection 'probably' spreading to cause sepsis and her death at age 62. The authors explicitly caution that a diagnosis of someone who died centuries ago can never be definitive because the surviving medical evidence is incomplete, and present the diabetes diagnosis as complementing — not overturning — the earlier consensus that she died of infection/erysipelas.
primary_source.access_note: lakartidningen.se, ynetnews.com, pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, en.wikipedia.org and the byteseu.com mirror are all EGRESS_BLOCKED in this sandbox; the Läkartidningen article's title, section, publication date, full author list with affiliations, methodology, hedging language and limitations were reconstructed from search-index extracts of the Läkartidningen page itself plus ynet's own English-edition report ('Israeli researcher helps solve 340-year mystery of Sweden's Queen Christina's death', ynetnews.com/health_science/article/h1109ljfgl). The paper's full running text was not read directly.
primary_source.subject_verified: Christina, Queen of Sweden (b. 8 December 1626, abdicated 6 June 1654, d. 19 April 1689 in Rome, aged 62). The headline's 'מלכת שבדיה' and 'שוויתרה על הכתר' match her uniquely — she is the Swedish queen famous for abdicating.
